subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find dy/dx if y = (sin x)ˣ + x^(sin x).

mark_split.label: Split y and take logarithms separately

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.204, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Long Answer question 2(i). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a CHAPTER-level marks banner (8M + 4M + 2 × 2M = 16M) but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split follows the shape this bank uses for a Maths-1B Section C question — two marks for the split and the logarithm move, two for each of the two derivatives, two for the sum. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. The mathematics was checked independently before writing: the boxed derivative agrees with a central difference quotient of (sin x)ˣ + x^(sin x) at x = 1 (1.236532246) and at x = 2 (−0.523278216), to nine decimal places at both points. Both test points have sin x > 0 and x > 0, which is the domain the two logarithms need.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what you do with the two terms before you differentiate anything, and why.

steps.label: Split y and take logarithms separately
steps.margin_note: First two marks. One mark for the split y = u + v, one for saying that logarithms are taken on u and on v one at a time. The logarithm of a sum does not open out, so a single logarithm of the whole of y leads nowhere.
steps.memory_tip: Two terms, two logarithms, two derivatives, then add. Never one logarithm for the whole of y.
lines: Let y = u + v,  where u = (sin x)ˣ  and  v = x^(sin x)
In each term the variable x stands in the base and in the power. The power rule needs a constant power and the exponential rule needs a constant base, so neither rule applies to either term.
So take logarithms of u and of v separately.
This requires sin x > 0 and x > 0, so that log(sin x) and log x exist.

recall.must_convey: That y is split as u + v and logarithms are taken on each term separately, because x stands in both the base and the power.
accept: put u equals sin x to the power x and v equals x to the power sin x
take log of each term separately and add the derivatives
x is in the base and in the power so use logarithmic differentiation
you cannot take the log of the sum, so split it first
rendu terms ni separate ga teesukoni log rasta
log of u and log of v one at a time, then add
heard_as: sin x to the power x

steps.why: A logarithm turns a power into a product, which is the only way to differentiate a term whose base and power both contain x. The split comes first because log(u + v) is not log u + log v.
common_mistakes: Writing log y = log[(sin x)ˣ + x^(sin x)] and then splitting it as log of the first term plus log of the second.
Using the power rule on (sin x)ˣ as if the power x were a constant.
Using the exponential rule on x^(sin x) as if the base x were a constant.

steps.label: Differentiate the first term
steps.margin_note: Two marks. One for log u = x log(sin x), one for the differentiated line. The right side is a product of x and log(sin x), so the product rule is used once.
steps.memory_tip: Multiplying back by u is the last move of every logarithmic differentiation. If u is missing from the answer line, a mark is missing with it.
lines: Taking logarithms,   log u = x · log(sin x)
Differentiating both sides with respect to x,
∴ du/dx = (sin x)ˣ [log(sin x) + x cot x]

recall.must_convey: That log u = x log(sin x), and that differentiating gives du/dx = (sin x)ˣ [log(sin x) + x cot x].
accept: log u is x times log sin x, then use the product rule
the derivative is sin x to the power x into log sin x plus x cot x
differentiate both sides and multiply back by u
cos x by sin x is written as cot x
log u equals x log sin x ani rasi, product rule vaadatha
one by u into du by dx equals log sin x plus x cot x

steps.why: The right side x · log(sin x) is a product, so the product rule applies, and the chain rule on log(sin x) supplies (cos x)/(sin x). Multiplying back by u is what turns (1/u)(du/dx) into du/dx itself.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply back by u = (sin x)ˣ, so the answer is left as a bracket only.
Differentiating log(sin x) as 1/(sin x) and dropping the cos x that the chain rule supplies.

steps.label: Differentiate the second term
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The product is the other way round here: sin x multiplies log x, so the derivative of the sine comes first and the 1/x comes second.
steps.memory_tip: In u the power was x and the base was sin x; in v the two are swapped. Writing log v = sin x · log x puts that swap on the page.
lines: Taking logarithms,   log v = sin x · log x
Differentiating both sides with respect to x,
(1/v)(dv/dx) = cos x · log x + sin x · (1/x)
∴ dv/dx = x^(sin x) [cos x · log x + (sin x)/x]

recall.must_convey: That log v = sin x · log x, and that differentiating gives dv/dx = x^(sin x) [cos x log x + (sin x)/x].
accept: log v is sin x times log x
the derivative is x to the power sin x into cos x log x plus sin x by x
product rule again, cos x log x plus sin x over x
multiply back by v at the end
log v equals sin x log x, product rule cheste vasthundi
here the base is x so the second part is one by x

steps.why: The same method is used a second time, on a product whose two factors are exchanged. Keeping it as a separate line is what stops the two brackets being mixed up when they are added.
common_mistakes: Writing log v = x · log(sin x), which is the first term's logarithm written twice.
Losing the 1/x that comes from differentiating log x.

steps.label: Add the two derivatives
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Each bracket must keep its own outside factor. The two brackets share no factor, so this two-bracket form is the final form.
steps.memory_tip: Each bracket stays attached to the term it came from: the (sin x)ˣ bracket holds cot x, the x^(sin x) bracket holds log x.

lines.text: ∴ dy/dx = (sin x)ˣ [log(sin x) + x cot x] + x^(sin x) [cos x · log x + (sin x)/x]

recall.must_convey: That the two derivatives are added, each keeping its own outside factor, and that no further simplification is possible.
accept: add the two derivatives to get dy by dx
sin x power x bracket plus x power sin x bracket
the answer is the sum of the two results
each bracket keeps its own factor in front
rendintini kalipithe dy by dx vasthundi
no more simplification, that is the final form
heard_as: du by dx plus dv by dx

steps.why: Differentiation runs term by term over a sum, so the two results are simply added. The two brackets have no common factor, which is the sign that the answer is already in its shortest form.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the two brackets together instead of adding them.
Putting one factor in front of both brackets, which changes both terms.

insider_note: TWO terms, each with x in base and power, so take logarithms of each SEPARATELY — logging the sum is not allowed. Differentiate u and v apart and add at the end.
